stem: A dataset had direct identifiers (names, SSNs) removed before being used for FM fine-tuning, but a privacy audit later shows individuals can still be re-identified by combining quasi-identifiers like ZIP code, birth date, and gender that remained in the data. What does this indicate about the anonymization approach used?

choices.text: Simple removal of direct identifiers is insufficient; techniques addressing quasi-identifiers (such as generalization, k-anonymity, or suppression of combinations of fields) are needed to prevent re-identification
The data was already fully anonymized and the audit finding is a false positive
Encrypting the dataset at rest would have prevented this
This risk only applies to structured data, not text used for fine-tuning

explanation: Removing only direct identifiers is a common anonymization pitfall since combinations of quasi-identifiers can still uniquely re-identify individuals, motivating techniques like k-anonymity or generalization. Encryption at rest doesn't address in-use data containing re-identifying combinations, and the risk applies equally to structured and unstructured data.

stem: A healthcare support assistant must retain the ability for support agents to reference a patient's phone number for callback purposes, but must never expose the patient's full Social Security number in any generated response. When configuring PII handling in Bedrock Guardrails, what is the appropriate configuration?

choices.text: Configure the SSN entity type with the Block behavior and the phone number entity type with the Mask (or allow) behavior
Configure both entity types with Block so neither ever appears
Disable PII filtering entirely and rely on manual agent review
Configure both entity types with Mask using the identical masking character so they look the same in output

explanation: Guardrails lets you configure PII handling per entity type, so highly sensitive types like SSN can be blocked entirely while operationally needed types like phone number can be masked or allowed. Blocking both removes needed functionality, disabling filtering defeats the control, and identical masking doesn't fully block SSNs specifically.

stem: A hospital's generative AI application needs to mask internal patient identifiers (a custom 8-digit format unique to the hospital's systems) in generated summaries, but Bedrock Guardrails' built-in PII entity types do not include this custom identifier format. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer to detect the hospital's custom identifier format, and use it in a pre/post-processing step alongside Guardrails' built-in PII types
Wait until AWS adds this exact entity type to Guardrails before doing anything
Use only the built-in SSN entity type since it is numeric
Manually review every generated summary before release

explanation: When a sensitive pattern is organization-specific and not covered by built-in PII types, Comprehend supports training a custom entity recognizer that can be layered alongside Guardrails' standard PII handling. Waiting indefinitely leaves the gap unaddressed, the SSN type won't match a different format, and fully manual review doesn't scale as a systemic control.

stem: A governance team wants a standardized document that captures a fine-tuned model's intended use, risk rating, training data description, and evaluation results, to support internal review and audits. Which AWS capability provides this?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
AWS Glue Data Catalog

explanation: SageMaker Model Cards provide a structured way to document a model's intended uses, risk rating, training details, and evaluation results for governance and audits. CloudTrail records API activity, Guardrails enforces runtime safety, and the Glue Data Catalog stores dataset metadata, none of which serve as model documentation artifacts.

stem: A financial services company fine-tunes a foundation model using data that passes through several AWS Glue ETL jobs before landing in the training bucket. Auditors need to trace exactly which raw source tables and transformations contributed to the final training dataset. Which capability supports this?

choices.text: AWS Glue lineage tracking (data lineage visualization across Glue jobs and the Data Catalog)
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
SageMaker Model Cards alone
Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding

explanation: AWS Glue provides data lineage capabilities that track how data flows and transforms across Glue jobs and catalog entries, letting auditors trace a dataset back to raw sources. CloudWatch Logs Insights is for operational log analysis, Model Cards document the model rather than data lineage, and grounding check is a runtime accuracy feature unrelated to lineage.

stem: A team already uses the SageMaker Model Registry to version models and gate deployment approvals. A governance stakeholder asks why they also need SageMaker Model Cards. What is the best justification?

choices.text: The Model Registry tracks model versions and deployment approval status, while Model Cards capture qualitative and risk-related documentation (intended use, limitations, ethical considerations, evaluation results) that the registry does not natively provide; the two are complementary
Model Cards replace the need for the Model Registry entirely
Model Cards and the Model Registry are the same feature under different names
The Model Registry cannot be used with foundation models, so Model Cards are the only option

explanation: The Model Registry and Model Cards are complementary: the registry manages versioning and deployment approval workflow, while Model Cards provide governance-focused narrative documentation. They are not interchangeable, and the registry can be used with models derived from foundation models as well.

stem: A company ingests documents from multiple business units into a Bedrock Knowledge Base and needs to track and later query which sensitivity classification (public, internal, confidential) each source document had, for governance reporting. What is an effective approach?

choices.text: Tag/classify source objects and their corresponding AWS Glue Data Catalog table or partition metadata with sensitivity-level attributes, and reference those tags in governance reports
Rely on the FM to infer sensitivity from document content at query time
Store sensitivity level only in the chatbot's system prompt
Use Amazon CloudFront cache headers to mark sensitivity

explanation: Applying structured metadata tags at the Glue Data Catalog level creates a queryable, auditable record of each source's classification that governance reporting can rely on. Inferring sensitivity at query time is unreliable, system prompts aren't durable metadata, and CloudFront headers are unrelated to data governance.

stem: An auditor asks which IAM principal invoked a specific Bedrock foundation model on a given date, but a query of CloudTrail management events shows no matching entries. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

choices.text: InvokeModel calls are recorded as CloudTrail data events, not management events; the team must enable data event logging for Bedrock in the relevant CloudTrail trail
CloudTrail does not support Amazon Bedrock at all
The invocation must have used an IAM user instead of a role, which CloudTrail cannot log
CloudTrail only retains logs for 24 hours

explanation: Bedrock InvokeModel calls are logged as CloudTrail data events, which are not captured by default and must be explicitly enabled, unlike management events logged by default. CloudTrail does support Bedrock and logs both users and roles, and default retention is much longer than 24 hours.

stem: A compliance requirement states that every answer produced by a Bedrock Knowledge Base-powered assistant must be traceable back to the specific source document, version, and ingestion date. Which combination of practices best satisfies this at the data layer?

choices.text: Tag each ingested document with source, version, and ingestion-date metadata in the Glue Data Catalog (or equivalent metadata store) and enable Knowledge Bases citations so responses can be linked back to the tagged source chunks
Rely on the FM's response text alone to state where the information came from
Store all documents in a single untagged S3 prefix and use file names as the only tracking mechanism
Enable CloudTrail data events only, with no document-level metadata

explanation: Robust source attribution requires structured metadata captured at ingestion plus citations enabled at query time so each statement traces to a specific, versioned source chunk. Trusting the FM's self-reported sourcing is unreliable, file names alone aren't durable structured metadata, and CloudTrail alone tracks API calls, not document provenance.

stem: A large enterprise with dozens of AWS accounts under AWS Organizations wants to centrally prevent any account from invoking foundation models that have not been through a legal/compliance review, regardless of individual account IAM policies. What is the most effective control?

choices.text: A Service Control Policy (SCP) applied at the relevant Organizational Unit that denies bedrock:InvokeModel for any model ARN not on the approved list
An IAM policy applied individually in each of the dozens of accounts
A Bedrock Guardrail applied only in the production account
A CloudWatch alarm that notifies security after an unapproved model is used

explanation: SCPs set an organization-wide permission boundary that overrides individual account IAM policies, making a single SCP the most centralized and reliable way to enforce this across many accounts. Per-account IAM policies must be replicated separately, a single-account guardrail doesn't cover other accounts, and a CloudWatch alarm is detective, not preventive.

stem: An enterprise is deciding between (1) a centralized shared-services account through which all teams access Bedrock via cross-account roles, versus (2) letting each of 20 teams manage its own direct Bedrock access in their own accounts. From a governance perspective, what is the main tradeoff?

choices.text: Centralized access simplifies consistent policy enforcement, auditing, and cost visibility but can introduce an onboarding bottleneck and require robust cross-account role design, while per-team access is more autonomous but risks inconsistent guardrails and fragmented audit trails across 20 accounts
There is no meaningful governance difference between the two approaches
Per-team accounts always provide better security because they use separate accounts
Centralized access removes the need for IAM entirely

explanation: Centralizing access via a shared-services account eases consistent guardrails, cost allocation, and auditing at the cost of potential onboarding friction and role complexity, while decentralized access trades consistency for autonomy and fragmented auditability. The other options deny any real tradeoff or make incorrect absolute claims.

stem: A governance team wants continuous, automated verification that every Bedrock Agent deployed across the organization has a Guardrail attached, flagging any agent that does not. What AWS service is best suited to continuously evaluate this configuration compliance?

choices.text: AWS Config with a custom or managed rule that checks Bedrock Agent configurations for an associated guardrail
Amazon Macie
AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon Comprehend

explanation: AWS Config is designed for continuous evaluation of resource configurations against defined rules, well-suited to flag Bedrock Agents lacking a required guardrail association. Macie discovers sensitive data, Glue crawlers infer schema, and Comprehend performs NLP, none of which evaluate resource configuration compliance.

stem: A team has fine-tuned a foundation model used for loan-eligibility summarization and wants ongoing production monitoring for both (a) whether the statistical distribution of incoming requests is drifting from the training data, and (b) whether the model's fairness/bias characteristics are drifting over time for protected groups. Which two SageMaker Model Monitor capabilities should they enable? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Data quality monitoring
Bias drift monitoring
Contextual grounding check
Denied topics monitoring
Prompt attack detection

explanation: Model Monitor's data quality monitor detects drift in incoming inference data relative to a baseline, and its bias drift monitor (built on SageMaker Clarify) tracks changes in bias metrics for protected attributes over time, matching both needs. Contextual grounding check and prompt attack detection are Bedrock Guardrails features, and denied topics monitoring is not a distinct Model Monitor capability.

stem: Security notices an unusual spike in requests that are being blocked by Bedrock Guardrails' prompt-attack filter from a small set of source IP addresses/API keys over a short window, suggesting automated jailbreak probing. What is the most appropriate real-time response mechanism to configure going forward?

choices.text: Publish Guardrails intervention metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers automated throttling or notification when blocked-request rates from a single identity exceed a threshold
Manually review CloudTrail logs once per quarter
Increase the model's context window to accommodate more requests
Disable the guardrail to reduce log noise

explanation: Real-time misuse detection requires near-real-time signals, which CloudWatch alarms on Guardrails intervention metrics provide, enabling automated throttling or alerting as the spike happens. Quarterly manual review is far too slow, increasing context window is unrelated, and disabling the guardrail removes the very control that detected the attack.

stem: A team is weighing real-time CloudWatch alarms on Guardrails intervention rates against a weekly batch review of aggregated invocation logs for governance monitoring. What is the main advantage of the real-time approach that the periodic approach lacks?

choices.text: Real-time alarms enable rapid detection and response to an active abuse pattern as it happens, minimizing the window of exposure, whereas a weekly batch review only surfaces the issue after it may have already caused harm
Weekly batch review is always more accurate than real-time monitoring
Real-time alarms eliminate the need for any log retention
Periodic review cannot be automated at all

explanation: The core advantage of real-time monitoring is reduced time-to-detection and response for active threats, which a weekly cadence cannot match. Batch review isn't inherently more accurate, real-time alarms don't eliminate the value of retained logs, and periodic review can also be automated, just with longer detection latency.

stem: A product team is deciding whether to expose the full Bedrock Agent reasoning trace directly to end customers in a customer-facing app, versus keeping it available only to internal support staff via a separate audit view. What is the main risk of exposing the raw trace to end customers?

choices.text: The trace may reveal internal tool names, system prompts, data sources, or intermediate reasoning that could leak sensitive implementation details or be exploited to craft better prompt injection attacks
Traces are always encrypted and therefore inherently safe to expose to anyone
Exposing traces to customers automatically improves model accuracy
Traces cannot be generated at all for customer-facing applications

explanation: Raw agent traces often contain internal implementation details that could help an attacker craft targeted prompt injection or reveal proprietary system design, so a curated internal view is generally safer for customer-facing apps. Encryption in transit doesn't make content safe to display broadly, exposing traces has no effect on model accuracy, and traces can be generated for customer-facing agents regardless of who sees them.

stem: An FM-powered agent that looks up order status and issues refunds gives a customer an incorrect refund amount. The team needs to determine whether the error occurred in the FM's reasoning, a specific tool/action group call, or the underlying data. What is the most effective debugging approach?

choices.text: Review the Bedrock Agent trace for that invocation to inspect each reasoning step, the exact parameters passed to each action group/tool, and the tool's returned data, isolating where the incorrect value was introduced
Re-run the same prompt multiple times and average the refund amounts
Immediately retrain the entire foundation model
Disable the refund tool permanently

explanation: The agent trace gives step-by-step visibility into reasoning, tool invocations, and returned data for a specific request, directly enabling root-cause isolation. Re-running and averaging doesn't diagnose root cause, retraining the whole FM is disproportionate for one bug, and disabling the tool removes functionality without fixing the issue.

stem: A team building a traditional tabular credit-risk model needs to explain individual feature contributions to each prediction, while a separate team building a Bedrock multi-step agent needs to explain its tool-use reasoning. Which pairing of tools is correctly matched to each need?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify (e.g., SHAP-based feature attribution) for the tabular model, and Bedrock Agents trace for the agent's reasoning steps
Bedrock Agents trace for both use cases
SageMaker Clarify for both use cases
Amazon Comprehend for both use cases

explanation: SageMaker Clarify provides feature-attribution explainability suited to traditional ML models like tabular credit-risk models, while Bedrock Agents trace explains a generative agent's orchestration reasoning, matching each tool to a different model paradigm. Using either tool for both would be a mismatch, and Comprehend is an NLP service, not an explainability tool for either scenario.

stem: A data science team wants to check for imbalance in a training dataset's representation of different demographic groups before any model is trained, as an early fairness check. What category of SageMaker Clarify metric addresses this stage?

choices.text: Pre-training bias metrics (e.g., measuring class imbalance or label distribution differences across groups in the dataset)
Post-training bias metrics measured on model predictions
Feature attribution drift metrics from Model Monitor
Contextual grounding scores from Bedrock Guardrails

explanation: SageMaker Clarify's pre-training bias metrics evaluate the dataset itself before a model is trained, matching this early-stage check. Post-training metrics evaluate predictions after training, feature attribution drift is a post-deployment monitoring concept, and grounding scores relate to RAG accuracy, not dataset fairness.

stem: Before fully replacing a production customer-service FM with a newly fine-tuned version, a team wants empirical evidence that the new model performs at least as fairly and effectively across different customer segments before a full rollout. What approach best supports this?

choices.text: Run an A/B test routing a controlled portion of live traffic to the new model versus the current model, and compare quality and fairness metrics across segments before deciding on full rollout
Replace the model for 100% of traffic immediately and monitor for complaints
Only test the new model in a lab environment with a handful of manually chosen examples
Skip evaluation since the new model was fine-tuned on more recent data

explanation: A/B testing with controlled traffic allocation provides real-world comparative evidence on quality and fairness while limiting risk, the standard safe approach before full rollout. Immediate full replacement removes the ability to compare or roll back safely, a small manual sample lacks rigor, and newer training data doesn't guarantee fairness.

stem: A team needs to evaluate whether a customer-facing FM's generated responses show inconsistent tone or helpfulness across different customer name/demographic cues embedded in otherwise-identical prompts, across tens of thousands of generated samples. Manual human review of all samples is not feasible. What approach is most appropriate at this scale?

choices.text: Use an LLM-as-a-Judge approach, where a separate (often larger or specialized) foundation model scores each response against defined fairness/consistency criteria, with periodic human spot-checks to validate the judge model's own reliability
Have a single engineer manually read all tens of thousands of samples
Skip fairness evaluation since manual review is infeasible
Use only aggregate sentiment scores from Amazon Comprehend as a complete fairness assessment

explanation: LLM-as-a-Judge lets a capable model apply consistent scoring criteria at scale, while periodic human spot-checks validate the judge model isn't introducing its own biases. Manual full review is infeasible as stated, skipping evaluation is unacceptable, and aggregate sentiment alone doesn't capture consistency across demographic cues.

stem: SageMaker Clarify post-training bias analysis reveals that a fine-tuned model's approval recommendations show a significant disparate impact against one demographic group compared to others, holding qualifications constant. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Investigate root cause in the training data and fine-tuning process (e.g., rebalancing training examples, adjusting the fine-tuning approach), and consider complementary runtime controls, then re-evaluate with Clarify before redeployment
Immediately deploy the model to production and monitor customer complaints as the primary fairness check
Simply increase the Bedrock Guardrails hate speech filter strength
Ignore the finding since Clarify metrics are only advisory and not actionable

explanation: A significant disparate impact finding calls for investigating and addressing root causes in data/training, followed by re-evaluation before redeployment. Deploying with only complaint-based monitoring lets harm occur first, a hate-speech filter is unrelated to disparate impact in approvals, and disparate impact findings should be acted on, not dismissed.

stem: A team is deciding whether to fully replace human fairness reviewers with an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline for evaluating generated content at scale. What is the key risk of full replacement that argues for retaining some human-in-the-loop review?

choices.text: The judge model itself can carry its own biases or blind spots inherited from its training data, potentially systematically mis-scoring the same categories of content it is supposed to catch, so periodic human validation of the judge's outputs helps detect and correct this
LLM-as-a-Judge is always slower than human review, so there is no scale benefit
Human reviewers are legally required for every single generated output under all AWS service terms
LLM-as-a-Judge cannot be used with Amazon Bedrock models

explanation: A judge model is itself an FM that can carry systematic biases, risking consistent mis-scoring of certain content categories that goes undetected without human validation, the core motivation for a hybrid approach. LLM-as-a-Judge is generally faster and more scalable, there is no blanket AWS requirement for human review of every output, and judge techniques can use Bedrock-hosted models.

stem: A company's responsible-AI policy prohibits its generative AI products from generating content that promotes competitors' products by name or gives medical diagnoses. Which Bedrock Guardrails configuration most directly operationalizes this policy at runtime?

choices.text: Define denied topics for 'competitor product promotion' and 'medical diagnosis,' described in natural language, and attach the guardrail to all relevant model invocations
Rely solely on the SageMaker Model Card documenting the policy
Add a comment in the source code referencing the policy document
Increase the maximum token limit for responses

explanation: Denied topics let an organization encode specific prohibited subject areas directly into a runtime-enforced guardrail applied to every invocation, the direct technical enforcement mechanism. A Model Card documents but doesn't enforce policy at runtime, a code comment has no functional effect, and token limits are unrelated to topic restriction.

stem: An external auditor wants evidence that a company's generative AI product both (a) is documented with its intended use, limitations, and risk assessment, and (b) technically enforces the organization's content policy at runtime. Which combination of artifacts should the team present?

choices.text: The SageMaker Model Card for the model (documentation) together with the Bedrock Guardrails configuration (denied topics, content filters) attached to the application (runtime enforcement) and relevant CloudTrail logs showing the guardrail is actually invoked
Only the SageMaker Model Card, since documentation alone satisfies both requirements
Only the Bedrock Guardrails configuration, since runtime enforcement alone proves intended use was documented
A general company privacy policy PDF unrelated to the specific model

explanation: Satisfying both the documentation and runtime enforcement requirements requires presenting the Model Card alongside the actual Guardrails configuration and evidence such as CloudTrail logs that it is applied in practice; each artifact alone covers only half the requirement. A generic company policy document provides no model-specific evidence for either requirement.

stem: The legal team issues an urgent policy update requiring all customer-facing generative AI applications company-wide to immediately stop discussing a newly restricted topic. The company has 15 separate applications, each currently referencing its own independently configured Bedrock Guardrail. What is the most efficient way to roll out this change reliably across all 15 applications?

choices.text: Update a shared/centrally managed guardrail configuration (or use infrastructure-as-code to push the same denied-topic update to all 15 guardrails) rather than manually editing each one independently
Manually log into each of the 15 application consoles and edit each guardrail one at a time with no tracking
Wait for each application team to notice the policy email and update their own guardrail whenever convenient
Disable all 15 applications until further notice

explanation: Centralizing guardrail configuration or using infrastructure-as-code lets a single policy change roll out reliably and quickly across many applications, reducing inconsistency or missed updates. Manual, untracked edits across 15 consoles are error-prone, waiting on individual teams risks delayed compliance, and disabling all applications is an unnecessary overreaction.

stem: A new engineer asks why the team maintains both Bedrock Guardrails and SageMaker Model Cards when both seem related to 'responsible AI.' Which statement best explains the distinct role each plays?

choices.text: Guardrails actively enforce policy at runtime by filtering prompts and responses in real time, while Model Cards passively document the model's intended use, limitations, and evaluation results for governance and audit purposes; neither substitutes for the other
Guardrails and Model Cards perform the exact same function and either one alone is sufficient
Model Cards actively block harmful content in real time just like Guardrails
Guardrails are only used for documentation, not runtime filtering

explanation: Guardrails are an active, runtime enforcement mechanism, whereas Model Cards are a passive documentation artifact capturing governance-relevant information; together they cover enforcement and documentation respectively. The other options incorrectly conflate the two or reverse their actual functions.

stem: A company runs a multi-tenant GenAI SaaS platform on Amazon Bedrock and needs to attribute token usage and cost to individual customer accounts for chargeback billing. Which approach provides the most accurate token-level attribution with the least custom infrastructure?

choices.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging with request metadata tags for each API call, then aggregate the logged inputTokenCount and outputTokenCount fields in CloudWatch Logs Insights or an S3-based analytics pipeline, grouped by the metadata tag
Rely on AWS Cost Explorer cost allocation tags applied to the Bedrock service, which report token counts at the per-customer level automatically
Use CloudTrail management events to capture InvokeModel calls, since these include per-request token consumption details
Query Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation job reports, which include cumulative token usage broken down by tenant

explanation: Model invocation logging captures per-request token counts and supports custom request metadata that can tag calls by tenant, enabling precise chargeback aggregation. Cost Explorer surfaces service-level cost rather than per-tenant token counts, CloudTrail management events don't include token usage, and Model Evaluation reports are for quality metrics, not billing.

stem: A RAG chatbot passes retrieved passages plus the last 10 turns of conversation history into a 128K-context model on every request. Latency and cost have grown as conversations lengthen. Which change most directly reduces token consumption without materially harming answer quality?

choices.text: Summarize/compress older conversation turns into a rolling summary and only keep the most recent 2-3 turns verbatim, while keeping full retrieved context
Switch to a model with an even larger context window so the growing history no longer causes errors
Increase the number of retrieved passages so the model has more grounding regardless of conversation length
Disable the retrieval step for turns after the first user message

explanation: Summarizing stale conversation turns is a standard context-window optimization/prompt-compression technique that trims token count while preserving essential grounding. A larger context window increases cost without solving the underlying inefficiency, and adding more passages or disabling retrieval either worsens cost or degrades quality.

stem: An engineering team notices that a document-summarization pipeline sends the same lengthy system prompt (containing formatting instructions and few-shot examples) with every request, consuming a large share of input tokens and cost. The team wants to cut input-token cost without changing the underlying model or degrading output consistency. Which two actions should they take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the static prefix portion of the prompt so repeated tokens are billed at a reduced cached rate
Move the few-shot examples and formatting instructions into a shorter, distilled instruction set or a fine-tuned model, reducing the static prompt length itself
Increase the temperature parameter to shorten generated output
Switch the request to streaming mode to reduce token billing
Add more few-shot examples to improve consistency

explanation: Prompt caching lets a model bill repeated static prefixes at reduced cost/latency, and shortening the reusable instruction/example block directly reduces the recurring token count. Temperature and streaming don't affect billed token counts, and adding more examples increases tokens rather than reducing them.

stem: A product team is choosing a foundation model tier for a customer support triage feature that classifies incoming tickets into one of eight categories and drafts a short reply. Which model-selection strategy best balances cost and capability within a tiered-usage framework?

choices.text: Route the classification step to a smaller, cheaper model and reserve a larger, more capable model only for drafting the reply when the ticket is flagged as complex or ambiguous
Use the largest available foundation model for every step to guarantee the highest possible accuracy on both classification and drafting
Use the smallest available model for both steps to minimize cost, regardless of drafting quality
Randomly alternate between a small and large model on each request to average out cost and quality

explanation: A tiered-usage framework routes simpler, well-bounded tasks like classification to smaller/cheaper models and escalates to larger models only when task complexity justifies the added cost. Always using the largest model overspends, always using the smallest risks poor draft quality, and random routing ignores actual task complexity signals.

stem: A team evaluates two models for a summarization workload: Model A costs $0.003/1K input tokens and $0.015/1K output tokens with 92% human-rated quality; Model B costs $0.0008/1K input tokens and $0.0016/1K output tokens with 85% human-rated quality. Requests use 2,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens at 5 million requests/month, and the acceptable quality threshold for this use case is 80%. What is the most defensible cost-optimization decision?

choices.text: Select Model B, since it clears the 80% quality bar at dramatically lower cost, and reserve Model A only for a smaller subset of requests that fail an automated quality check
Select Model A for all requests because higher quality is always worth the added cost regardless of the use case's quality bar
Select whichever model has the lower per-token output price alone, ignoring input token pricing
Alternate between both models evenly across all requests to average total spend

explanation: Since both models exceed the acceptable quality threshold, routing the bulk of traffic to the cheaper model and escalating only flagged low-confidence outputs to the higher-cost model reflects the cost-capability tradeoff a tiered framework recommends. Always choosing the higher-cost model regardless of the quality bar wastes budget, and ignoring input pricing or averaging spend ignores the real per-request economics.

stem: A media company needs to generate alt-text descriptions for 2 million product images by the end of the week, but the workload is not latency-sensitive and can tolerate results arriving asynchronously within 24 hours. Which approach minimizes cost while meeting the requirement?

choices.text: Submit the workload as an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job, which processes large volumes of prompts asynchronously at a lower per-token price than on-demand real-time inference
Provision Bedrock Provisioned Throughput sized for peak real-time traffic and send all 2 million requests through synchronous InvokeModel calls
Send all 2 million requests concurrently through the on-demand InvokeModel API to finish as quickly as possible
Split the workload across multiple AWS Regions using cross-region inference to reduce cost per request

explanation: Amazon Bedrock batch inference is designed for large, non-latency-sensitive workloads and offers reduced pricing compared with on-demand real-time invocation. Provisioned Throughput is priced for sustained high-volume real-time traffic and would cost more here, blasting synchronous on-demand calls maximizes cost and risks throttling, and cross-region inference primarily addresses throughput/availability rather than batch cost efficiency.

stem: A production application invoking a custom fine-tuned model on Amazon Bedrock experiences frequent ThrottlingException errors during business hours, even though on-demand throughput quotas were recently increased. Requests are consistent and predictable in volume from 9 AM to 6 PM daily. What is the most effective fix?

choices.text: Purchase Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput sized to the predictable peak demand for the business-hours window, since custom models require Provisioned Throughput for reliable, dedicated capacity
Continue requesting on-demand quota increases indefinitely until throttling stops
Add exponential backoff retry logic only, without changing the underlying capacity model
Move the workload to AWS Lambda to bypass Bedrock's throughput limits entirely

explanation: Custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock generally require Provisioned Throughput for reliable inference at scale, and sizing a commitment to the known predictable peak window resolves capacity-driven throttling. Repeated quota requests and retry-only strategies don't address the underlying capacity requirement, and Lambda cannot bypass Bedrock's own throughput enforcement.

stem: A team is deciding between Amazon Bedrock prompt caching and a custom semantic cache built on a vector store for a document Q&A application where every request reuses the same 6,000-token system prompt and document context, but the user's question changes each time. Which statement correctly compares the two approaches for this scenario?

choices.text: Prompt caching directly reduces cost and latency for the repeated static prefix on every call, while a semantic cache would need to key on the varying question and would not reliably hit since each question differs
A semantic cache is strictly superior because it can cache entire responses regardless of prompt structure
Prompt caching and semantic caching solve identical problems and are interchangeable in this scenario
Prompt caching only works with edge locations and cannot be used for API-based model invocation

explanation: Because the static portion is identical across calls but the question varies, prompt caching is well-suited to discount the repeated prefix, whereas a semantic cache keyed on full-response similarity would rarely match since the question content differs each time. Prompt caching operates directly through Bedrock's inference API, not exclusively through edge locations.

stem: A GenAI-powered product-description generator produces a fixed catalog of pre-generated descriptions that rarely change once created, and these are served to a global e-commerce audience. Which caching layer most effectively reduces latency and repeated compute cost for this specific workload?

choices.text: Cache the generated descriptions at edge locations using Amazon CloudFront so subsequent global requests are served from a nearby cache without re-invoking the model
Re-invoke the foundation model on every page view to guarantee freshness
Use Bedrock Provisioned Throughput exclusively without any caching layer
Use semantic caching keyed on real-time user session data

explanation: Since the content is static once generated, caching it at CloudFront edge locations minimizes latency and eliminates redundant model invocations for repeat views worldwide. Re-invoking the model per view wastes cost, and Provisioned Throughput or semantic caching address different problems, not static content delivery.

stem: A conversational assistant currently waits for the entire model response to complete before displaying anything to the user, resulting in a perceived multi-second delay for long answers. Which change most improves perceived responsiveness without changing the underlying model or infrastructure capacity?

choices.text: Enable response streaming so tokens are displayed to the user incrementally as they are generated
Reduce the max_tokens parameter to force shorter answers regardless of content needs
Increase the model's temperature to generate responses faster
Move the client application closer to the model endpoint using edge caching

explanation: Streaming delivers tokens to the client as they're generated, dramatically improving perceived latency even though total generation time is unchanged. Reducing max_tokens truncates useful content, temperature doesn't affect generation speed, and edge caching doesn't apply to dynamic per-request generation.

stem: A voice assistant requires sub-500ms time-to-first-token for a natural conversational experience, but the current general-purpose foundation model averages 900ms time-to-first-token under normal load. The use case tolerates a modest reduction in reasoning depth. What is the best combination of actions to meet the latency target?

choices.text: Switch to a latency-optimized inference option or a smaller/distilled model variant tuned for low time-to-first-token, and pre-compute or cache responses for the most frequent conversational intents
Increase the max_tokens limit so the model can think longer before responding
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt to improve response quality, accepting the added latency
Switch exclusively to Provisioned Throughput without changing the model or prompt design

explanation: Combining a latency-optimized or smaller model with pre-computed responses for common intents directly targets time-to-first-token, the responsiveness bottleneck described. Increasing max_tokens or adding few-shot examples increases prompt/generation length and latency, and Provisioned Throughput alone addresses throughput/availability rather than per-request first-token latency for an inherently slower model.

stem: A RAG application backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector index has grown to hold 40 million document chunks. Query latency for k-NN retrieval has degraded significantly, and recall has also dropped for some queries. Which combination of actions is most likely to restore both retrieval latency and accuracy?

choices.text: Re-tune the HNSW index parameters (such as ef_search, m, and ef_construction) and consider index sharding or increasing node/OCU capacity to match the larger corpus size
Reduce the embedding dimensionality to zero to eliminate vector search entirely and rely on keyword search only
Increase the number of documents returned per query (top-k) without changing index configuration
Switch to storing embeddings as plain text fields and perform brute-force cosine similarity in the application layer

explanation: As a vector index grows, its approximate nearest-neighbor parameters and underlying compute/shard capacity often need retuning and scaling to maintain recall and latency at the new scale. Eliminating vector search loses semantic retrieval quality, increasing top-k alone adds noise without fixing the index, and brute-force similarity would be far slower at this scale.

stem: A legal-document search assistant using RAG must retrieve results for queries that include exact statute numbers, precise legal terms, and semantically similar concepts expressed in different wording. Purely semantic (dense vector) retrieval has been missing exact statute-number matches. What is the best retrieval strategy?

choices.text: Implement hybrid search that combines dense vector similarity with sparse/keyword (BM25) matching and merges the ranked results, so exact terms and semantic matches are both captured
Switch entirely to keyword-based BM25 search and drop vector search altogether
Increase the chunk size for embeddings so more context is captured per vector
Only use vector search but increase the similarity threshold to be more permissive

explanation: Hybrid search combines exact lexical matching with semantic vector similarity, directly addressing the failure mode of missing precise terms like statute numbers while retaining semantic recall. Dropping vector search loses conceptual matching, larger chunks don't fix exact-term recall, and loosening the similarity threshold increases noise rather than solving exact-match misses.

stem: A data science team needs to score 500,000 customer reviews for sentiment using a foundation model, with results needed by tomorrow morning but no requirement for individual real-time responses. Which throughput optimization approach is most appropriate, and why?

choices.text: Use Amazon Bedrock batch inference, since it is designed to maximize throughput for large offline workloads at lower cost than issuing 500,000 individual synchronous calls
Issue individual synchronous InvokeModel calls in a tight loop from a single Lambda function to keep the implementation simple
Provision maximum on-demand quota and fire all requests concurrently to finish as fast as possible regardless of cost
Use response streaming for each request to reduce the total processing time

explanation: Batch inference is purpose-built for large-volume, non-real-time workloads and offers better throughput economics than issuing many individual synchronous calls. A single Lambda looping through calls is inefficient and may hit execution time limits, maximizing concurrent on-demand calls risks throttling and higher cost, and streaming addresses perceived latency for single interactive requests, not bulk throughput.

stem: An application generating long-form reports observes that overall throughput (reports per minute) is far below expectations even though the model's Provisioned Throughput capacity appears sufficient on paper. Investigation shows most requests specify max_tokens far higher than the actual typical output length, and many responses include verbose boilerplate the team doesn't need. What is the most effective fix to improve effective throughput?

choices.text: Right-size max_tokens closer to realistic output needs and tighten the prompt/system instructions to eliminate unnecessary boilerplate, reducing output token generation time per request
Increase the Provisioned Throughput commitment further even though capacity already appears sufficient
Reduce the number of concurrent requests sent to the endpoint
Increase the temperature parameter to make generation faster

explanation: Output token generation time dominates FM latency/throughput, so trimming unnecessarily high max_tokens ceilings and removing boilerplate directly reduces per-request generation time and raises effective throughput. Adding more provisioned capacity doesn't help if each request is individually slow, reducing concurrency lowers total throughput further, and temperature has no effect on generation speed.

stem: A code-generation assistant must produce syntactically consistent, deterministic-looking output for the same prompt across repeated runs, while a separate creative marketing-copy generator should produce varied, novel phrasing across runs. Which parameter adjustments correctly support both use cases?

choices.text: Set a low temperature (and/or low top-p) for the code-generation assistant to favor high-probability, consistent tokens, and a higher temperature (and/or higher top-p) for the marketing-copy generator to increase output diversity
Set a high temperature for both use cases, since higher temperature always improves output quality
Set top-k to zero for both use cases to disable sampling entirely
Use the same default temperature for both use cases since parameter tuning has no measurable effect on output determinism

explanation: Lower temperature/top-p narrows the sampling distribution toward the most likely tokens, producing consistent output suited to code generation, while higher temperature/top-p broadens sampling for creative diversity. Uniformly high temperature would hurt code correctness, and claiming these parameters have no effect is incorrect.

stem: A team tuning a creative-writing model finds that a high temperature setting alone sometimes produces incoherent or nonsensical output because low-probability tokens are occasionally sampled. They still want creative diversity but need to prevent selection of extremely unlikely tokens. Which parameter adjustment best addresses this?

choices.text: Combine the high temperature with a top-p (nucleus sampling) or top-k constraint that limits sampling to a restricted set of higher-probability tokens, filtering out the long tail of implausible choices
Lower the temperature to zero, which eliminates all creativity but guarantees coherence
Increase max_tokens so the model has more room to self-correct after an implausible token
Set top-p to 1.0 and top-k to the maximum possible value to include the widest possible token pool

explanation: Combining temperature with top-p/top-k caps the candidate token pool to more probable options, preserving diversity while excluding the low-probability tail responsible for incoherent output. Zero temperature removes creativity entirely, increasing max_tokens doesn't undo an already-sampled bad token, and maximizing top-p/top-k widens rather than narrows the implausible tail.

stem: A GenAI application built on Amazon SageMaker real-time inference endpoints serves a workload with a predictable daily traffic pattern: near-zero traffic overnight, a sharp ramp at 8 AM, sustained peak from 9 AM to 5 PM, and a decline after 6 PM. The team wants to minimize cost while still meeting a strict SLA during business hours. What is the best resource-allocation strategy?

choices.text: Configure SageMaker inference auto scaling with target-tracking policies tied to invocation/utilization metrics, combined with scheduled scaling actions that pre-warm capacity ahead of the known 8 AM ramp
Provision a fixed instance count sized for peak traffic and run it unchanged 24/7
Provision the minimum possible instance count at all times and rely solely on reactive scaling with no pre-warming
Manually resize the endpoint capacity by an on-call engineer at fixed times each day

explanation: Combining auto scaling with scheduled/predictive scaling that pre-warms capacity before a known traffic ramp minimizes idle-period cost while still meeting SLA during the predictable peak. A fixed peak-sized deployment wastes cost overnight, purely reactive scaling risks SLA breaches during the sharp ramp due to scale-up lag, and manual resizing doesn't scale operationally.

stem: A SageMaker real-time endpoint hosting a foundation model is configured with target-tracking auto scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance, but during sudden traffic spikes users experience elevated latency and some request failures for several minutes before additional instances become available and healthy. What change would most directly reduce this scaling-lag impact?

choices.text: Reduce the scale-out cooldown period and lower the target threshold so scaling triggers earlier, and maintain a minimum baseline of warm instances (or use SageMaker Inference Components) rather than scaling from a minimal baseline
Increase the scale-in cooldown period, since scale-in behavior is responsible for scale-out lag
Switch to Provisioned Throughput on Bedrock instead of addressing the SageMaker endpoint's scaling configuration at all
Disable auto scaling entirely and run a single, very large instance permanently

explanation: Lowering the scale-out target/cooldown and keeping a warm baseline (or using faster-provisioning constructs) reduces the gap between a spike and new capacity becoming available, directly addressing scaling lag. Scale-in cooldown affects capacity removal, not addition; switching services doesn't fix the SageMaker endpoint's configuration; and a single oversized instance eliminates elasticity and increases idle cost.

stem: A team is deciding between Amazon Bedrock on-demand throughput, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, and a self-managed SageMaker inference endpoint for a new GenAI feature with highly variable and still-unpredictable traffic in its first three months post-launch. Which option is most appropriate initially, and why?

choices.text: Start with Bedrock on-demand throughput, since it requires no capacity commitment and scales elastically with actual usage, then evaluate Provisioned Throughput once traffic patterns become predictable enough to justify a capacity commitment
Commit to Bedrock Provisioned Throughput immediately to guarantee the lowest possible per-token cost regardless of traffic uncertainty
Build and manage a custom SageMaker endpoint from day one since it always provides better cost efficiency than managed Bedrock inference
Avoid measuring traffic patterns altogether and choose capacity based solely on the largest anticipated burst

explanation: On-demand throughput avoids locking into a capacity commitment while traffic is still unpredictable, and Provisioned Throughput becomes cost-effective only once sustained, predictable volume justifies it. Committing early or building a custom endpoint prematurely risks paying for unused or misallocated capacity, and sizing purely for the largest anticipated burst ignores cost efficiency during normal periods.

stem: A platform team wants a baseline set of operational metrics to monitor the health of a production GenAI application built on Amazon Bedrock. Which set of metrics most directly supports holistic operational observability, as opposed to model-quality evaluation?

choices.text: Request latency (including time-to-first-token), invocation error/throttling rates, token throughput, and endpoint/service availability
Only the model's hallucination rate as measured by periodic human review
Only the number of foundation models available in the selected AWS Region
Only the cost per token as reported monthly in the AWS Cost and Usage Report

explanation: Holistic operational observability centers on system health signals like latency, error/throttling rates, throughput, and availability, which reveal infrastructure and service-level problems in near real time. Hallucination rate is a quality metric rather than an operational one, model availability by Region isn't a runtime health metric, and monthly cost reports are too coarse and delayed for operational monitoring.

stem: A finance team wants near-real-time alerting when token consumption for a specific application spikes unexpectedly, which could indicate a prompt-injection loop, a runaway agent, or a client-side bug. Which approach best supports this monitoring requirement?

choices.text: Publish token usage metrics from Bedrock model invocation logs to Amazon CloudWatch as custom metrics and configure a CloudWatch alarm, potentially using anomaly detection, to notify the team when consumption deviates significantly from the historical baseline
Review the AWS Cost and Usage Report once per month to check for unusual token-driven cost spikes
Rely solely on the foundation model's built-in Guardrails to prevent all excessive token usage automatically
Manually query Bedrock model invocation logs in the console once a week

explanation: Streaming token usage into CloudWatch custom metrics and using an anomaly-detection-based alarm enables near-real-time detection of abnormal consumption patterns. A monthly cost report or weekly manual log review is far too infrequent, and Guardrails address content safety/policy enforcement, not runaway token consumption detection.

stem: A team wants to continuously monitor hallucination rates for a production RAG application without relying solely on periodic manual human review, which is too slow to catch regressions after a prompt or knowledge-base change. Which combination of capabilities most directly supports automated, ongoing hallucination monitoring at production scale?

choices.text: Use Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks (or an equivalent automated groundedness/faithfulness scoring step) on live responses against retrieved source context, logging scores to a monitoring dashboard and alerting when the ungrounded-response rate crosses a threshold
Perform a single one-time human evaluation before launch and assume hallucination rates remain constant afterward
Rely exclusively on user-reported complaints as the sole signal for hallucination detection
Disable retrieval augmentation, since removing RAG eliminates the possibility of hallucination

explanation: Automated groundedness/contextual-grounding checks can score live responses against retrieved evidence continuously and feed a monitoring/alerting pipeline, catching regressions in near real time. A one-time pre-launch evaluation and user complaints are both lagging, incomplete signals, and removing RAG does not eliminate hallucination and would likely worsen factual grounding.

stem: Leadership wants a single operational dashboard that shows GenAI application health (latency, error rate), cost trends (token spend by application), and compliance signals (Guardrails intervention counts) in one place for daily review. Which AWS approach best supports this consolidated view?

choices.text: Build a unified Amazon CloudWatch dashboard, or an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace backed by CloudWatch and OpenSearch data sources, that combines operational metrics, cost-related custom metrics derived from token usage, and Guardrails intervention metrics into one set of widgets
Require leadership to check three separate, disconnected tools (billing console, a spreadsheet of latency numbers, and raw Guardrails logs) each day
Rely only on the default Bedrock console home page, which does not support custom cross-service dashboards
Export all data to a single static PDF generated once per quarter

explanation: A consolidated CloudWatch dashboard, optionally via Amazon Managed Grafana for richer visualization, can combine operational, cost-derived, and compliance/Guardrails metrics from multiple sources into one integrated view for daily review. Manually checking disconnected tools or a quarterly static PDF defeats the goal of a real-time consolidated view, and the default console home page isn't designed for custom cross-metric dashboards.

stem: A regulated healthcare GenAI application must demonstrate that every user-facing model output that triggered a Guardrails intervention, such as blocked PII or a denied topic, is logged with enough detail for an auditor to review later. Which AWS capability most directly supports this compliance monitoring requirement?

choices.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and configure invocation logging so that intervention events, including the guardrail action taken and relevant context, are captured and retained, for example in CloudWatch Logs or S3, for audit review
Rely on the default request/response payload without enabling any logging, since Bedrock retains this data indefinitely by default
Use only client-side browser logs on the end user's device to capture Guardrails interventions
Disable Guardrails logging to reduce storage cost, since compliance review can be reconstructed from memory afterward

explanation: Enabling Guardrails together with model invocation logging captures a durable, retrievable record of intervention events suitable for audit, satisfying the compliance monitoring requirement. Bedrock does not retain full request/response data indefinitely without logging enabled, client-side logs are not authoritative audit evidence, and disabling logging removes the exact evidence auditors need.

stem: An agentic GenAI application invokes several external tools, a search API, a database-query tool, and a code-execution tool, as part of multi-step reasoning. End-to-end task success rate has dropped, but the team isn't sure whether the foundation model's tool-selection reasoning or one of the individual tools themselves is failing. What is the best way to isolate the root cause?

choices.text: Instrument each tool invocation separately with its own success/failure rate, latency, and error-type metrics, in addition to overall task success, so degradation in a specific tool can be distinguished from degradation in the model's tool-selection or argument-generation logic
Only monitor the overall end-to-end task success rate, since that single number is sufficient to diagnose any root cause
Assume the foundation model is always the cause of any agentic workflow failure and retrain or replace it first
Remove monitoring from individual tools entirely to reduce operational overhead

explanation: Per-tool performance metrics alongside overall task success let the team distinguish a failing tool from flawed model reasoning about tool selection or arguments, which a single aggregate metric cannot do. Assuming the model is always at fault or removing tool-level monitoring both eliminate the diagnostic granularity needed to isolate the actual root cause.

stem: A production RAG system uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as its vector store. Over several months, ingestion has grown substantially, and the operations team wants to proactively manage the vector store's health rather than reacting to outages. Which set of practices best reflects sound vector store operational management?

choices.text: Monitor OpenSearch Compute Unit (OCU) utilization, indexing/query latency, and storage growth trends; set alarms on capacity thresholds; and periodically review and prune or re-index stale/duplicate embeddings as the corpus evolves
Monitor only the total dollar cost of the OpenSearch Serverless collection once per quarter
Never re-index or prune embeddings, since vector stores are designed to grow indefinitely without operational maintenance
Rely exclusively on the RAG application's end-user error reports to detect vector store issues

explanation: Proactive vector store management requires tracking compute/capacity utilization, latency, and storage growth with alerting, plus periodic curation such as pruning stale or duplicate embeddings, to avoid degraded recall or performance over time. Quarterly cost-only checks, never maintaining the index, and waiting for end-user complaints are reactive or insufficient practices that miss developing problems.

stem: A team is comparing Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension as the vector store for a new RAG application that also needs to join retrieved passages with existing relational customer records in the same query. From an operational-management perspective, which consideration most favors Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector for this specific use case?

choices.text: Aurora PostgreSQL allows vector similarity search to be combined with standard relational joins and existing operational tooling, such as existing backup, monitoring, and access-control practices for the relational database, in a single query, avoiding the need to operate and synchronize a separate dedicated vector store
Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector always provides lower query latency at any index size compared to a purpose-built vector search service
OpenSearch Serverless cannot store vector embeddings at all and is unsuitable for any RAG workload
Operational management is identical between the two options in every respect, so the choice should be made solely on licensing cost

explanation: When retrieved passages must be joined with existing relational data, using pgvector inside Aurora PostgreSQL avoids operating a second, separately managed vector store and reuses existing relational operational practices, a genuine operational advantage for this join-heavy use case. It is not universally true that pgvector is always faster at scale, OpenSearch does support a vector engine, and the two options are not operationally identical.

stem: After deploying a minor prompt-template change to a production summarization feature, the team suspects output quality regressed for certain document types, but has no formal way to confirm this before deciding whether to roll back. What is the best troubleshooting approach?

choices.text: Run the new prompt template against a curated golden dataset of representative documents with known-good reference outputs, and perform systematic output diffing, combining automated similarity/quality scoring with targeted manual review, between the old and new template's outputs to quantify any regression before deciding on rollback
Roll back immediately without any comparison, based solely on a handful of informal user complaints
Keep the new prompt template in production indefinitely and wait to see if complaint volume changes over the next few months
Re-deploy the exact same new template again, assuming a second deployment will resolve any quality issue

explanation: A golden dataset with known-good references, combined with systematic output diffing between the previous and new prompt versions, gives an objective, repeatable basis for confirming and quantifying a regression before making a rollback decision. Rolling back on anecdote alone, waiting passively for complaint trends, or blindly re-deploying the same change all lack the rigor needed to properly troubleshoot a suspected FM output regression.

stem: A GenAI platform team is designing a quality framework to score chatbot responses before promoting a new model version to production. They want to measure three dimensions: whether the response addresses the user's question (relevance), whether factual claims in the response are correct (factual accuracy), and whether the model gives similar answers to semantically equivalent prompts (consistency). Which statement best describes how these three dimensions should be combined in an evaluation framework?

choices.text: The three dimensions are mutually exclusive, so only one should be measured per evaluation run to avoid conflating results.

Relevance, factual accuracy, and consistency should each be scored with a distinct metric and aggregated into a composite quality score, since a response can be relevant but factually wrong, or consistent but irrelevant.
Only factual accuracy needs to be measured because relevance and consistency are automatically implied by a high factual accuracy score.
Consistency should be dropped from professional evaluation frameworks because Bedrock Guardrails already enforces it.

explanation: Relevance, factual accuracy, and consistency are independent quality axes that a comprehensive framework must score separately before combining into a composite score, since strong performance on one does not imply strong performance on another. Guardrails filters content safety/policy issues, not response consistency, so option D is incorrect.

stem: A financial services company built a Bedrock-based application that summarizes quarterly earnings call transcripts. Before launch, the team needs an evaluation framework that specifically catches cases where the summary states a numeric figure (e.g., revenue growth) that does not appear in the source transcript. Which evaluation approach best targets this specific failure mode?

choices.text: Run a Bedrock automatic model evaluation job using only the built-in toxicity metric, since toxic language is the primary compliance risk.
Use a faithfulness or groundedness metric that checks whether every claim in the generated summary is supported by the source transcript, flagging unsupported numeric claims as hallucinations.
Rely solely on a BLEU score comparison against a single reference summary written by an analyst.
Measure only response latency, since factual correctness cannot be evaluated programmatically at a professional level.

explanation: A faithfulness or groundedness metric is designed to verify that generated claims are traceable to the source document, directly catching unsupported numeric hallucinations. Toxicity and latency are unrelated risk dimensions, and BLEU measures lexical overlap with a single reference rather than factual grounding.

stem: A team is choosing between an automatic model evaluation job and a human-based evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock to compare two candidate foundation models for a creative marketing copy generator. Which factor should most influence the decision to use a human-based evaluation job instead of an automatic one?

choices.text: Human-based evaluation is required whenever the evaluation dataset contains more than 1,000 prompts.
Automatic evaluation cannot be used with any Anthropic Claude models on Bedrock.

The quality dimension of interest, such as creative tone or brand-voice appropriateness, is subjective and difficult to capture with built-in or algorithmic metrics, so human judgment better captures nuanced preference.
Human-based evaluation is always cheaper and faster than automatic evaluation jobs.

explanation: Human-based evaluation is best suited to subjective, nuanced quality dimensions like tone or brand voice that built-in or algorithmic metrics struggle to score reliably. There is no dataset-size threshold forcing human evaluation, automatic evaluation works with Claude models, and human evaluation is typically slower and more costly, not cheaper and faster.

stem: An e-commerce company runs two prompt template variants (A and B) for a Bedrock-powered product-description generator, splitting live traffic 50/50 and measuring click-through rate as the success metric for two weeks. A stakeholder asks why the team did not instead rely solely on an offline Bedrock automatic model evaluation job comparing the same two prompts against a static test dataset. What is the most accurate justification for using a live A/B test in this case?

choices.text: Bedrock automatic evaluation jobs cannot process prompt templates, only raw model invocations.
A/B testing measures actual downstream business impact, such as click-through rate, under real user behavior and traffic conditions, which a static offline dataset evaluation cannot capture.
A/B testing is required because offline evaluation datasets are limited to 100 prompts maximum.
A/B testing eliminates the need for any further human or automatic evaluation once it concludes.

explanation: Live A/B testing captures real user behavior and business outcomes that a fixed offline dataset cannot represent, making it the appropriate complement to offline evaluation for business-impact metrics. The other options misstate Bedrock evaluation capabilities or overstate what A/B testing replaces.

stem: A GenAI-powered internal knowledge assistant lets employees click a thumbs-up or thumbs-down icon after each answer. The product team wants to use this signal to catch quality regressions after each biweekly prompt template update, in addition to automated metrics. Which practice best operationalizes this user-centered feedback for ongoing quality assurance?

choices.text: Discard the feedback data after 24 hours since user ratings are only useful for real-time monitoring dashboards, not longer-term analysis.

Log each rating together with the associated prompt version, retrieved context, and response into a durable store, then track thumbs-down rate by prompt version over time and trigger a review when the rate exceeds a defined threshold after a release.
Use only the aggregate thumbs-up percentage across the assistant's entire lifetime as the single go/no-go gate for every new release.
Convert thumbs-down feedback directly into new Guardrails denied topics without further review.

explanation: Persisting ratings with version metadata and tracking the trend per release is what lets the team detect a regression tied to a specific prompt update. A lifetime aggregate would dilute a recent regression, discarding data loses the ability to trend it, and auto-converting feedback into guardrail policies without review risks incorrect or unsafe configuration.

stem: Two weeks after launching a rating widget on a GenAI chatbot, the product team notices that fewer than 2 percent of conversations receive any thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback, making the signal too sparse to detect quality regressions reliably. Which change would most directly increase the statistical usefulness of this user feedback mechanism without introducing significant bias?

choices.text: Only prompt users for feedback after conversations the model itself scores as low-confidence, and use that subset as the sole quality signal for the entire user base.

Increase the visibility and reduce the friction of the rating control, for example an always-visible inline rating after every response, and supplement it with periodic, randomly sampled in-app micro-surveys, so coverage increases across representative traffic rather than only opt-in users.
Require users to submit a rating before they can send their next message, regardless of context.
Replace user ratings entirely with an LLM-as-a-Judge score, since human feedback volume is inherently too low to be useful.

explanation: Lowering friction and adding randomly sampled prompts increases feedback coverage while keeping the sample representative of overall traffic. Sampling only low-confidence conversations biases the signal toward a non-representative subset, forced ratings degrade UX, and abandoning human feedback in favor of a judge model discards a distinct and valuable signal rather than fixing the coverage problem.

stem: A team maintains a Bedrock Knowledge Bases-backed support bot and updates its system prompt roughly every two weeks. To prevent a prompt change from silently degrading answer quality on previously well-handled questions, which quality assurance process should be built into the deployment pipeline?

choices.text: A regression test suite of curated question-answer pairs with expected outcomes that is automatically re-run against every new prompt version before promotion, comparing scores against the previous baseline.
A one-time manual review performed only during the bot's initial launch.
Relying exclusively on production user complaints as the sole detection mechanism for quality issues.
Disabling evaluation entirely for prompt-only changes since only foundation model swaps require testing.

explanation: An automated regression suite run before every promotion is the standard continuous-QA pattern for catching silent degradations introduced by prompt changes. The other options are one-time, purely reactive, or wrongly assume prompt-only changes carry no risk.

stem: After promoting a new prompt template version, a nightly regression test job reports that overall aggregate accuracy stayed flat at 92 percent, so the release was not rolled back. A week later, users report that a specific category of questions about refund policy now fails almost every time. Investigating, the team finds the regression suite's 200 test cases include only 4 refund-policy questions, diluted among many easier categories. What is the most effective structural fix to the regression testing process going forward?

choices.text: Increase the total number of unrelated easy test cases so the aggregate score becomes more stable.

Stratify the regression suite so each meaningful question category, including refund policy, has a statistically adequate sample and is scored and gated separately, in addition to the overall aggregate, so a category-specific regression cannot be masked by an unrelated majority.
Remove the refund-policy category from the suite since it is clearly a low-priority edge case.
Lower the passing threshold for the aggregate score so future regressions are caught sooner.

explanation: Stratifying by category with independent pass or fail gates prevents a severe regression in a small but important category from being averaged away by a large, unaffected majority. Adding more easy cases worsens the dilution, removing the category eliminates visibility entirely, and lowering the aggregate threshold does not address the underlying masking problem.

stem: A team building a Retrieval Augmented Generation application on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases wants an evaluation that separately reports whether the retriever returned passages relevant to the user's query and whether the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved passages. Which pair of RAG evaluation metrics addresses these two concerns respectively?

choices.text: Toxicity and latency

Context relevance, which measures whether retrieved chunks are pertinent to the query, and faithfulness or groundedness, which measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context
BLEU score and token count
Model temperature and top-p

explanation: Context relevance evaluates retrieval quality and faithfulness or groundedness evaluates whether generation stays grounded in the retrieved context, matching the two stated concerns exactly. The other pairs are either unrelated safety and performance metrics or generation hyperparameters, not RAG evaluation metrics.

stem: A team evaluating a customer-facing chatbot needs to score thousands of open-ended responses for helpfulness and coherence on a nightly basis, a task too large to review manually and too nuanced for exact-match or keyword-based scoring. They configure a Bedrock evaluation job that uses a separate, more capable foundation model to read each prompt-response pair and output a numeric quality score with a rationale. What evaluation technique does this describe, and what is its key limitation compared to human evaluation?

choices.text: This is A/B testing; its key limitation is that it requires live production traffic.

This is LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; its key limitation is that the judge model can inherit its own biases or blind spots, so its scores may not fully align with actual human preference and should be periodically validated against human ratings.
This is regression testing; its key limitation is that it can only compare against a fixed golden dataset.
This is embedding-based similarity scoring; its key limitation is that it cannot process natural language rationale.

explanation: Using a separate, more capable foundation model to score and explain quality at scale is the LLM-as-a-Judge pattern, whose main caveat is potential judge-model bias or misalignment with actual human preference, requiring periodic human calibration. The other labels do not match a model scoring another model's outputs with rationale.

stem: A professional services firm must choose an evaluation strategy for a Bedrock-based contract-review assistant that flags risky clauses. Compliance requires high confidence in correctness, but the volume of contracts reviewed each week, over 5,000, makes exhaustive human review of every output impractical. Which evaluation strategy best balances rigor and scale for this scenario?

choices.text: Use LLM-as-a-Judge to score 100 percent of outputs at scale for consistency and clause-detection quality, then route a statistically sampled or low-confidence subset to qualified human reviewers for validation and periodic recalibration of the judge model's alignment.
Use only human review for 100 percent of outputs regardless of volume, since compliance risk justifies unlimited reviewer headcount.
Use only LLM-as-a-Judge with no human involvement at any stage, since the judge model is itself a foundation model and therefore authoritative.
Skip evaluation entirely and rely on Bedrock Guardrails to catch any risky clauses before they reach the assistant's output.

explanation: A hybrid strategy scales judge-based scoring across full volume while reserving human review for a validating sample, satisfying both scale and compliance-grade rigor. Pure human review does not scale to the described volume, pure LLM-as-a-Judge lacks independent validation for a compliance context, and Guardrails is a content-safety control rather than a correctness or quality evaluation mechanism.

stem: A team wants to route a sample of low-confidence responses from their Bedrock agent to qualified human reviewers for labeling, then feed the corrected labels back into their evaluation dataset to improve future prompt and retrieval tuning. Which AWS service is designed to implement this kind of human review workflow with minimal custom infrastructure?

choices.text: Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I), which provides built-in human review workflows that can route model outputs to a private, vendor, or Amazon Mechanical Turk workforce and capture structured reviewer input
AWS X-Ray, which is designed for distributed tracing rather than human review workflows
